newsitem.title: POLAND: French, German, Polish foreign ministers in talks.
newsitem.headline: French, German, Polish foreign ministers in talks.

text.p: The French, German and Polish foreign ministers met in Warsaw on Thursday to keep up the momentum of their cooperation in the so-called Weimar Triangle, a framework Poland views as a key to European integration.

"This is a meeting which I hope will add impetus to contacts within the Weimar Triangle," Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski told a news conference after receiving the ministers in his Warsaw palace.
He said France's Herve de Charette and Germany's Klaus Kinkel had confirmed the heads of state of the three countries would meet next year, although a date had yet to be fixed.

The ministers, who also met Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, told a news conference they had agreed on instituting cooperation among their ambassadors in Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Ukraine and Belarus.
They also backed a French proposal for a permanent conference providing a forum for dialogue between the 15 European Union members and 11 associated states.
Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said earlier that they planned to examine how to apply and extend the successful model of Franco-German ties to relations between Bonn and Warsaw.

Another aim was to discuss European security including the planned expansion of NATO, which Poland wants to join, and ways of involving countries which could not or would not enter the Western alliance soon, he said on Wednesday.
Poland wants to be more involved in discussing the pattern of future economic and monetary union in the European Union, which it also aspires to enter.
"It is our goal to build a joint position of the three countries around these matters," said Rosati, whose country aims to enter monetary union not long after joining the EU.
This was the sixth annual meeting of the three countries' foreign ministers under the triangular relationship, launched in Weimar, Germany, in August 1991.

Poland views the axis, which France has backed with greater enthusiasm since President Jacques Chirac visited Warsaw in September, as an important symbol because it straddles former World War Two and Cold War divisions.
